claims.claim: Shinto is the indigenous religious tradition of Japan, centered on devotion to invisible spiritual beings and powers called kami, to shrines, and to rituals.
Kami are sacred or divine presences — spirits, forces of nature, or elements of the landscape — and are not gods in the Western sense; even the translation "spirits" oversimplifies the concept.
Shinto has no founder and no canonical scriptures; it teaches ethical principles without commandments and does not require exclusive adherence.
Scholars commonly distinguish shrine Shinto (jinja), sect Shinto, and folk Shinto as forms of the tradition.
State Shinto was a historical development within shrine Shinto during the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, tied to the Japanese state, and it came to an end after World War II.
Shinto practice centers on shrines: purification rites (harae), offerings, prayer, and festivals (matsuri); the torii gate marks the shrine boundary, and many shrines offer omikuji paper fortunes.
Hatsumode, the first shrine visit of the New Year, is the most popular shared Shinto practice in Japan; Shinto rites also mark weddings and other life events.

The Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, compiled in the early eighth century, are the earliest surviving myth-histories of Japan and are studied as historical sources for Shinto's early development; they are named but never quoted in this lesson.
Shinto and Buddhism have coexisted and blended in Japan for over a millennium; at various periods kami were understood as protectors or manifestations of buddhas.
Shinto remains an active tradition today, with shrines maintained across Japan and Shinto rites marking national and personal occasions.
Introductory sociology textbooks present Shinto as an example of animism — belief in the divinity of nonhuman beings such as animals, plants, and natural objects — practiced by some Japanese people.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether kami should be translated as "gods" or "spirits."
positions: Popular usage and some nineteenth-century translations render kami as "gods."
Scholars prefer "spirits" or "sacred/divine powers," noting that "gods" implies transcendent deities unlike kami.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: This lesson describes kami as sacred or divine presences and explicitly notes they are not gods in the Western sense, following Britannica and BBC Religions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether state Shinto is best described as a distinct form of Shinto or as a historical state policy within shrine Shinto.
positions: Some popular descriptions treat state Shinto as one of Shinto's major forms.
Britannica describes it as a now-defunct development within shrine Shinto of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents state Shinto factually as a historical development that ended after World War II, without political analysis; deeper treatment belongs to the religion-and-politics topic.
